passages.t: The nations of the land: ‘devote them to complete destruction’
passages.happening:
Moses speaks of the day Israel enters Canaan. God will drive out before it seven peoples, ‘seven nations larger and stronger than you’ (verse 1).

When God has given them into Israel's hand, the command is this: “then you must devote them to complete destruction. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy” (verse 2).

Two more commands follow. Israel is not to marry among them: “Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (verses 3-4). And Israel is to destroy the places of their worship: ‘tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their idols in the fire’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The seven names are an old list of the peoples of Canaan. Some are well known from ancient records. Others are known mainly from the Bible. Seven is a number of completeness in Scripture, and the list stands for the whole population of the land.

The words ‘devote them to complete destruction’ translate the Hebrew word herem, the ban. Under the ban a city and its people were given over wholly. The victors kept no plunder and took no slaves. Israel did not invent the practice. Mesha, a king of Moab, boasted on his monument around 840 BC that he had devoted an Israelite town to his own god, and he used the same word.

A reader must take verse 2 at its weight. It commands the destruction of peoples. The hard question below does not look away from that.

The same passage also says things that sit strangely beside a total destruction. It forbids treaties with these peoples and marriage with their sons and daughters. Those commands assume that the peoples will still be there. Later in the chapter Moses says they will be driven out ‘little by little’ (verse 22).

The reason given is about worship and not about race. The danger named is that Israel's children will be turned ‘to serve other gods’. Marriage in the ancient world was not a private matter. It joined families, and it usually brought the gods of each house into the new home. The Old Testament itself shows that the concern was faith and not blood. Rahab, a Canaanite of Jericho, and Ruth, a woman of Moab, are both welcomed into Israel, and both stand in the family line of King David.

The objects in verse 5 are known from the ancient world. Sacred pillars were standing stones at shrines. Asherah was a goddess, and the poles were wooden signs of her worship. When verse 5 spells out what Israel is to do, it names their altars, pillars, poles and idols.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua records that Rahab and her whole family were spared: “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

Exodus speaks of the same peoples being moved out slowly: “Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you” (Exodus 23:30). And near the end of Joshua's life God says to him, ‘very much of the land remains to be possessed’ (Joshua 13:1).

Jesus, in the same land centuries later, commanded, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that would not receive him, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).
passages.hard:
Did God command Israel to destroy whole peoples? How do Christians read it?

The command is in the text. Verse 2 says, ‘devote them to complete destruction’, and verse 16, ‘Do not look on them with pity.’ It is among the most troubling passages in the Bible, and the Bible itself teaches a reader to feel the objection: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers” (24:16). Abraham asked God, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25), and was not rebuked.

Christians who receive these books as God's word read the command in several ways, as the site's pages on the conquest set out. Each has a cost.

Some read the language of total destruction as the stock idiom of ancient war, which the same books qualify, since Canaanites are still in the land in Joshua and Judges. The cost is that this eases the scale and not the substance.

Some read it as judgment on named evil after long patience (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5; 12:31). The cost is the children, for whom this reading has no answer that takes the grief away.

Some ground it in God's unique right over life, as Augustine and Thomas Aquinas did. The cost is that it does not show how anyone could know such a command was God's.

Some read these texts as God stooping to the understanding of an ancient people, to be seen through Christ. The cost is that the reader must decide which portraits of God to trust, and critics say this weakens the authority of Scripture.

Many hold more than one together. The site takes no side, and none of them makes the passage easy.

Under all of them these things hold. The command was tied to one land, one moment and seven named peoples, and it was never renewed. It was not about race. Israel is told it is no better (9:4-6), and the same ban falls on an Israelite who takes a devoted thing (verse 26) and on an Israelite town that turns to other gods (13:12-18). The New Testament gives the church no land to take and no people to destroy.

So it must be said plainly. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people. It names peoples who passed away long ago. It says nothing about any nation, state, land or conflict today. Christians did later quote these chapters over their own wars. That was a misuse of the text, and the church must own it as sin.

Nothing here permits contempt for the Canaanites or for anyone. God says, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: This is a passage to be honest with. Ask what troubles you in it, and say it to God as plainly as Abraham did. Then notice what the chapter fears most. It is not the strength of other peoples. It is that Israel's own heart will be drawn off to other gods. Ask what has that kind of pull on you, and what it would mean to break its altar and not make terms with it.

passages.happening:
Moses gives the reason behind the commands. “For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth” (verse 6).

Then he says why God chose them, and first he says what the reason was not. “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers, He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery” (verses 7-8).

So Israel is to know what kind of God this is: ‘the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments’ (verse 9). Those who hate him he repays (verse 10). “So keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances that I am giving you to follow this day” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘Holy’ means set apart. Israel is set apart to belong to God.

The word translated ‘prized possession’ comes from the world of kings. A related word in the language of Babylon was used for a king's private treasure, kept apart from the general wealth of his realm. David uses the Hebrew word for his own store of gold and silver. The whole earth belongs to God. Israel is his in a special and cherished way.

Then comes one of the most important sentences in the book. Why did God choose this people? A hearer might expect a reason that flatters: their numbers, their strength, their goodness. Moses rules out numbers here, and he will rule out goodness in chapter 9. Israel was ‘the fewest of all peoples’.

The reason he gives goes in a circle on purpose. God set his love on them because he loved them. There is nothing behind God's love except God's love, and the promise he had sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The word for ‘choose’ is the Old Testament's main word for election, and here it rests on nothing in the ones chosen.

Three things follow from this, and a reader should hold them together.

To be chosen is not to be better. The text says so in as many words.

To be chosen is to be set apart for a purpose and held to account. Israel was to be holy. God's promise to Abraham had the nations in view from the start: “and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).

And to be chosen gives no right to look down on anyone. This book commands Israel to love the foreigner (10:19). Nothing in this passage is contempt for other peoples, and nothing in it is a claim that any nation today may make for itself.

‘Loving devotion’ translates the Hebrew chesed. It is love that keeps its promises, the loyalty of one who has bound himself to another. Verse 9 sets its reach at ‘a thousand generations’.
passages.later:
At Sinai God had first used the word: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” (Exodus 19:5).

The prophet Amos drew the hard side of being chosen: “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2).

Paul says of the Jewish people, his own, that ‘they are loved on account of the patriarchs. For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable’ (Romans 11:28-29).

Peter uses the words of this passage for those who belong to Christ: ‘a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession’ (1 Peter 2:9). Christians understand in different ways what that means for Israel, and the note on 1 Peter 2 sets out the views.

John gives the same order of love that Moses gives: “We love because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
passages.asks: God's love for Israel had no cause outside himself. Ask whether you think God loves you for a reason: your usefulness, your effort or your record. Then ask what would change if his love came first and rested on nothing in you. And if you know yourself chosen, ask whether it has made you humble or proud toward those outside.

passages.happening:
Moses sets out what will follow if Israel listens and keeps these laws. God ‘will keep His covenant and the loving devotion that He swore to your fathers’ (verse 12). “He will love you and bless you and multiply you” (verse 13). He will give children, grain, new wine and oil, calves and lambs.

There will be no childless man or woman among them, and none among their animals (verse 14). “And the LORD will remove from you all sickness. He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt” (verse 15).

Then the command of verse 2 is repeated. Israel must destroy the peoples God gives over to it, without pity, and must not worship their gods, ‘for that will be a snare to you’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The words ‘bless’ and ‘multiply’ in verse 13 go back to God's promises to Abraham. The good things listed are the plain goods of a farming people: children, harvests and healthy herds.

Grain, new wine and oil were the three staple crops of the land. The prophet Hosea later charged Israel with giving Baal the credit for them (Hosea 2:8). Moses says that they come from the LORD. Israel does not need the shrines it was just told to tear down.

These promises are made to a nation, about its life in its land under the covenant. They describe where a whole people's life is heading over time. They are not a rule for reading any one person's life. The hard question below takes this up.

Verse 16 returns to the nations. The note on verses 1 to 5 sets out how Christians read that command. Here the stress falls on the last words. The gods of the land will be ‘a snare’. A snare is a hidden trap for a bird or a small animal. Idolatry does not announce itself as the end of faith. It catches the foot.
passages.later:
The promise echoes what God said to Abraham at the beginning: “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you” (Genesis 12:2).

The book of Job is about a man of whom God himself says that he is ‘blameless and upright’ (Job 1:8), and who loses his children and his health.

When the disciples of Jesus asked whose sin had made a man blind, he answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).
passages.hard:
Verses 14 and 15 promise that no one will be childless and that sickness will be taken away. Does that mean a sick or childless person lacks faith or is being punished?

No. The promises are spoken to Israel as a nation in its land under the covenant of Sinai. The rest of the Bible refuses to turn them into a verdict on any one person. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah were all childless for years, and none of them is blamed for it. Job suffers though God calls him blameless. Jesus refuses the question of whose sin made a man blind.

The note on Leviticus 26, a chapter of the same kind, says what must be said here too. So this chapter is never God's verdict on your illness, your poverty, your childlessness or your loss. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Moses says that harvest and children are gifts of the LORD and not of any other god. Ask who or what you look to for the things you most need: security, a future and health. And if you carry an illness or a longing for a child, hear that this chapter is not a judgment on you.

passages.happening:
Moses knows what the people are thinking. ‘These nations are greater than we are; how can we drive them out?’ (verse 17).

His answer is memory. “But do not be afraid of them. Be sure to remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt” (verse 18). The God who did that will do the same again. He is among them, ‘a great and awesome God’ (verse 21).

It will not happen all at once. “The LORD your God will drive out these nations before you little by little” (verse 22). If the land emptied in a single stroke, wild animals would overrun it.

Last comes a warning about the idols. Israel must burn them and must not want the silver and gold on them, ‘or you will be ensnared by it’ (verse 25). Nothing of that kind may come into an Israelite house, ‘or you, like it, will be set apart for destruction’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The fear in verse 17 is the fear of Kadesh over again. Forty years earlier the parents had looked at the size of the peoples and refused to go in. Moses does not tell the children that the peoples are small. He tells them to remember Egypt. The answer to fear in this book is nearly always memory.

The ‘hornet’ of verse 20 has been read in more than one way: as real insects, as a picture of panic sent by God, or as an image of some foreign power that weakened Canaan before Israel came. The text does not explain it.

‘Little by little’ matters for how the whole chapter is read. Moses himself says the peoples of the land will not disappear in a day. The books of Joshua and Judges show them still there long afterward.

The last two verses turn the hardest word of the chapter back on Israel. The gold on an idol is tempting, and it looks harmless once the idol is gone. But a devoted thing brought home makes the one who takes it devoted too. The ban was never a mark of favor to one race. It could fall on an Israelite as readily as on a Canaanite. Joshua 7 tells of a man named Achan, on whom it did.

There is a warning here that outlasts its setting. Israel was in more danger from what it admired in Canaan than from Canaan's armies.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua tells what happened when the warning of verse 26 was ignored: “Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of what was set apart” (Joshua 7:1).

The book of Judges admits how partial the conquest was: “When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely” (Judges 1:28).

The risen Jesus sent his followers to the nations with a different charge: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19).
passages.asks: Moses answers fear by telling the people to remember. Ask what God has already done for you that you could set against the thing you are afraid of now. And think about the gold on the idol. Ask what you have kept from an old way of life because it seemed too good to throw out, and whether it has a hold on you.
